dialogue_history.sentences_no_utterance_types: Without strong state oversight, the private sector can cherry-pick profitable patients and ignore the vulnerable, which is why I believe government control of the NHS is non-negotiable. Innovation means nothing if half the population can’t afford it, so I’m convinced the government must step in to guarantee healthcare as a right, not a privilege. Without state intervention, inequality in healthcare access just widens, and I can’t accept a system where your wallet decides if you get treated. How can you justify reducing state oversight in healthcare when data from the ONS shows that private systems often prioritise profit over equal access for all? Competition in healthcare often drives up costs rather than quality, as private firms prioritise profit over patient needs.

second_speaker_utterance_with_correspond: ONS data on NHS funding cutting waiting times doesn’t hide the fact that the system still creaks with inefficiencies no cash can fully fix.
I reckon funding bloats a creaky system because red tape and poor management swallow up resources before they reach patients.
I’m certain enforcement in healthcare won’t fail the vulnerable because we’ve got hard proof from sectors like energy where tight rules stop firms screwing over the little guy.
Private firms won’t slip through cracks if we hit them with ruthless oversight, unlike the NHS where delays persist no matter the dosh.
Why do you keep dodging the reality that state control alone isn’t getting care to people fast enough?
